textClass.keywords: Glioma Tumor progression KLF14 FOSL1 Transcriptional inhibition

div.p: Background: Glioma, the most frequent central nervous system malignancy, is often promoted by the overexpression of Fos-like antigen 1 (FOSL1). However, the regulation of FOSL1 remains unexplored. The present study aimed to investigate the regulatory mechanism of FOSL1 to identify potential therapeutic targets for glioblastoma. Methods: This study's initial investigation utilized dual-luciferase reporter gene assays and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) assays to establish that Kruppel-like factor 14 (KLF14) inhibits the transcription of FOSL1. Subsequent immunohistochemistry and western blotting (WB) assays on glioma tissues confirmed a negative association between FOSL1 and KLF14. This study generated KLF14 knockdown cells and double knockdown cells of KLF14 and FOSL1 and further assessed cell growth through various experimental methods. The impact of KLF14 on tumor cell migration via FOSL1 was determined using qPCR and WB assays. A xenograft tumor model was utilized to verify tumor growth suppression by KLF14.

Results: The present study demonstrated that KLF14 restrains FOSL1 transcription and is inversely correlated with FOSL1 in glioma tissues. KLF14 overexpression was found to counteract FOSL1's effect on cell migration and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition in glioma cells, which coincided with decreased Snail2 and cluster of differentiation 44 (CD44) expressions. Further, KLF14 overexpression was shown to hinder tumor progression in vivo.

div.head: Conclusion:
div.p: This study highlights that FOSL1 is negatively regulated by KLF14 in glioblastoma and suggests that KLF14 overexpression can mitigate tumor growth by inhibiting FOSL1, thus identifying KLF14 as a novel molecular target for treating glioblastoma. Further research into the interplay and regulatory dynamics between KLF14 and FOSL1 under varying stress conditions can enhance the precision of glioblastoma treatment.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Glioma is the most common primary tumor of the central nervous system (CNS), accounting for more than 50 % of intracranial tumors [1]. The classical clinical treatment of glioma comprises surgery combined with radiotherapy and chemotherapy. However, glioma is characterized by a high degree of malignancy and the development of drug resistance. No therapeutic targets have been identified to date, making the treatment of glioma a worldwide public health challenge [2]. Therefore, identifying novel drug targets for glioma and exploring various effective treatment methods is paramount.

Fos-like antigen 1 (FOSL1) is a component of the transcription factor activator-protein-1 (AP-1) complex and is involved in cellular immune response regulation and tumor proliferation, migration, and invasion [3]. As a transcription factor of AP-1, FOSL1 activates bone matrix generation [4]. Overexpression of FOSL1 promotes the formation of osteosarcoma in mice [5]. FOSL1 acts as a potential downstream response factor of the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT) signaling pathway, thereby promoting cell invasion [6]. FOSL1 also functions as a proto-oncogene, regulating cell proliferation in Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog (KRAS)-dependent lung and pancreatic cancers [7]. A large-scale mass spectrometry study indicated that FOSL1 can be a potential marker and therapeutic target for treating CNS tumors [8]. However, FOSL1 regulation in CNS tumors remains unexplored, necessitating in-depth studies of the role of FOSL1 in CNS tumors, especially gliomas. The use of FOSL1 as a target for treating glioma requires investigating the regulation of FOSL1 in relation to glioma proliferation and the upstream regulatory mechanism of FOSL1.

KLF (Kruppel-like factor) transcription factors are a group of zinc finger proteins involved in gene transcription and play an important role in regulating cell proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis. The aberrant function of KLFs is closely related to the occurrence and development of tumors, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases, metabolic disorders, and other diseases [9]. Mammals possess 17 members of the KLF family (KLF1-KLF17), and the physiological and pathological functions of several KLFs have been studied extensively [10][11][12]. KLF14 was identified as a gene associated with fat metabolism and type II diabetes mellitus by genome-wide association analysis (GWAS) [13][14][15]. A study in 2011 extracted subcutaneous adipose tissue from 776 female twins and utilized it for whole genome analysis. The single nucleotide polymorphism rs473170 upstream of KLF14 was found to be associated with the expression of a large number of adipose genes; hence, KLF14 was named the "master switch of adipose metabolism" [16]. The KLF14 gene has more variants in humans than in other primates [17]. A study in 2015 identified for the first time that KLF14 was significantly associated with the occurrence and development of tumors, thereby considering it a new tumor suppressor [18]. KLF14 knockout in mice leads to the development of spontaneous tumors (spleen, thymus, lungs, etc.), and KLF14 knockdown significantly increases the grade of azoxymethane (AOM)/dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)-induced colon cancer progression. KLF14 deletion leads to excessive replication of centrosomes and thus induces genomic instability, an important cause of tumor occurrence and development [19,20]. Analysis of the Oncomine database showed significantly reduced transcription levels of KLF14 in various human cancer tissues. These studies demonstrate KLF14 to be a key factor in maintaining normal centrosome replication and genomic homeostasis and identify its significant association with tumorigenesis, tumor progression, and drug resistance. KLF14 is a tumor suppressor gene whose overexpression or increased activity facilitates tumor killing. However, no studies have elucidated the role of KLF14 in CNS tumors.

The present study demonstrated that KLF14 inhibited the transcription of FOSL1. KLF14 and FOSL1 are negatively correlated in glioma tissues. Overexpression of KLF14 reversed the effect of FOSL1 on cell invasion, migration, and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in glioma cells, accompanied by the downregulation of Snail2 and CD44.

Moreover, KLF14 overexpression inhibited tumor progression in vivo. Collectively, these results strongly validate that FOSL1 inhibition is a prognostic and therapeutic option for glioma. The study proposes KLF14 as a new tumor molecular marker and a potential target for treating glioma, thereby providing a novel target for anti-tumor drug research.

div.head: Cell culture and materials
div.p: The U87MG and U251MG cell lines were procured from the American Type Culture Collection. The cells were cultured in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10 % (v/v) fetal bovine serum (FBS). The coding sequences for KLF1-15 and FOSL1 were inserted into the pCDNA 3.0 vector or the pLVX-IRES lentiviral expression vector using standard molecular cloning techniques. Specific short hairpin ribonucleic acid (shRNA) primers and pLKO.1-puro lentiviral vectors were designed and acquired from Sangon Biotech (Shanghai, China). The synthesized oligonucleotides were subsequently annealed and ligated at the BstYI/EcoRI sites (New England Biolabs, MA, USA) of the pLKO.1-puro vector to generate pLKO.1-shFOSL1 and sh-KLF14 constructs. The sequences of shRNAs are listed below. The FOSL1-Si (shRNA) sequence was 5′-CCGGCCTCAGCTCATCGCAAGAGTACTCGA GTACTCTTGCGATGAGCTGAG.

GTTTTT-3'. The KLF14-Si (shRNA) sequence was 5′-CCGGTCATC-CAGATATGATCG AGTACTCGAGTACTCGATCATATCTGGATGATTTT TG-3'. Antibodies were purchased from Sigma (MO, USA) (FOSL1, GAPDH, and KLF14) and Proteintech (IL, USA) (Snail2 and CD44).

div.head: Cell transfections and infections
div.p: The assay was performed as previously reported [21]. The constructs were transfected into cells using polyethyleneimine (PEI) from Polysciences (PA, USA), adhering to the manufacturer's guidelines. The lentiviruses utilized in this study were generated following a standardized protocol. In summary, 5 μg of pMD2.G, 10 μg of PSPAX2, and 10 μg of constructs designed for the overexpression or knockdown of KLF14/FOSL1 were co-transfected into HEK293T cells cultured in a 100 mm dish with PEI. Lentiviral particles were harvested 48 h post-transfection. Subsequently, the infected cells were subjected to selection with 2-4 μg/mL of puromycin for two weeks to establish stably transfected cell lines. The efficiency of knockdown and overexpression were validated through quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) and western blot analysis.

div.head: Western blotting
div.p: Western blotting assay was performed as previously reported [18]. Cells were lysed in a lysis buffer composed of 50 mM Tris(hydroxymethyl)aminomethane hydrochloride (Tris-HCl) (pH 8.0), 5 mM ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), 150 mM sodium chloride (NaCl), 0.5 % nonylphenol ethoxylate (40) (NP-40), and 1 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF). Following lysis, the samples were centrifuged at 12,000 g for 10 min to remove insoluble debris. Cell lysates were further boiled in sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) sample buffer, fractionated by SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE), analyzed by western blotting using specific antibodies, and then developed using X-ray film in a dark box. The developed films were trimmed according to the bands and then scanned. The western blotting of tissues was carried out using formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) samples from six patients who were diagnosed with GBM at Linyi People's Hospital (Linyi, China). Paired tumor-adjacent normal tissue specimens were available in all six cases. All these samples were used for western blotting. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Linyi People's Hospital and performed following the declaration of Helsinki Principles. Informed consent was obtained from each participant.

div.head: Tissue microarray and immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining
div.p: Human tissue microarrays specific to glioma were obtained from Shanghai Superbiotek Pharmaceutical Technology Co., Ltd. Standardized IHC staining procedures were employed using antibodies directed against FOSL1 and KLF14. Five micrometer-thick sections were prepared from the paraffin-embedded tissue samples. These sections were immunolabeled with anti-human antibodies targeting KLF14 and FOSL1, following the application of an anti-mouse peroxidase kit, all in adherence to the protocols provided by the manufacturer. The staining intensities for FOSL1 and KLF14 were evaluated and assigned scores that were subsequently categorized into three levels: low (<5 points), medium (≥5 and ≤ 8 points), and high (≥9 and ≤ 12 points).

div.head: RNA extraction and quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR)
div.p: The assay was performed as previously reported [22]. Total RNA was extracted from tissues or cell lines utilizing the TRIzol reagent. The extracted total RNA was subsequently reverse-transcribed into complementary deoxyribonucleic acid (cDNA) employing the RevertAid First Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (Roche, Basel, Switzerland), following the manufacturer's guidelines. The synthesized cDNA was then subjected to quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) in triplicate using the StepOnePlus™ Real-Time PCR System running on an Applied Biosystems PCR machine (MA, USA). The relative expression levels of the specified genes were calculated using the comparative 2 -ΔΔCT method and normalized against β-actin. FOSL1 (forward): 5′-GCCTGTG CTTGAACCTGA-3′, FOSL1 (reverse): 5′-TGCTGCTACTCTTGCGATG-3'; β-actin (forward): 5′-GATCATTGCTCCTCCTGAGC-3′, β-actin (reverse): 5′-ACTCCTGCTTGCTGATCCAC-3'.

div.head: Cell growth analyses
div.p: Cell survival was determined using a cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) assay. Briefly, the proliferation of cells was quantified using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8, Dojindo Molecular Technologies, MD, USA) as per the instructions provided by the manufacturer. Briefly, the cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 1 × 10 4 cells/well and allowed to adhere overnight. At specific intervals (24, 48, and 72 h), CCK-8 solution was added to each well and incubated for 2 h at 37 • C. The absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader (Model, Company, Country). The experiments were performed in triplicate.

div.head: Clonal formation assay
div.p: A total of 1 × 10 3 FOSL1 overexpression or knockdown cells and control cells were respectively seeded in 12 well plates and cultured in a complete medium for 10 days. Later, cells were fixed with 4 % paraformaldehyde and stained with 0.1 % crystal violet. Following this, the clones per well were observed.

div.head: Transwell assay
div.p: Serum-starved cells were digested, counted, and diluted to a concentration of 1 × 10 5 cells per 100 μL. The lower chamber was filled with 600 μL of 20 % FFBS medium, while the upper chamber was filled with 100 μL of the diluted cells. After a 12-h incubation period, the cells were collected. All media in the upper and lower chambers were aspirated, and the chambers were washed thrice with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for 10 min each time. The cells were then fixed with methanol for 30 min, followed by two washes with PBS and drying. Each well in the lower chamber was stained with 0.1 % crystal violet solution for 30 min and then washed four times with PBS. Finally, images were taken under a microscope, and the cells were counted.

div.head: Luciferase reporter assay
div.p: A luciferase reporter assay was performed as previously reported [23]. The transcriptional activity of the FOSL1 promoter was monitored by subcloning -1000 -+ 200 bp of the FOSL1 promoter into pGL4.17. Further, a luciferase reporter assay was performed. The cells cultured in 24-well plates were co-transfected with the specified plasmids alongside the FOSL1-promoter luciferase reporter plasmid for 24 h. The luciferase activity was subsequently quantified utilizing the dual-luciferase assay kit (Promega, WI, USA). The pRL-TK plasmid was co-transfected to ensure normalization of transfection efficiency.

div.head: Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay
div.p: KLF14 chromatin immunoprecipitation was performed using Flag-M2 beads, and the coprecipitated chromatin was analyzed by PCR for the presence of the FOSL1 promoter DNA using 5′-GCCTGTGCTTGAACCTGA-3′ and 5′-TGCTGCTACTCTTGCGATG-3′ primers.

div.head: Tumor growth analysis in mice
div.p: The cells were subcutaneously injected into both flanks of male BALB/c nude mice (6-7 weeks old). Vector and KLF14 overexpression (OE) stable U251MG or U87MG cells (2 × 10 6 suspended in 100 μL PBS) were subcutaneously injected into each nude mouse (n = 6). The animals were euthanized using the cervical dislocation method when the tumor reached an endpoint size of ~1500 mm 3 or ~4 weeks after implantation. Animals were treated according to high ethical and scientific standards with oversight by the animal center at Guangzhou University of Chinese Medicine (certificate no: NH-IACUC-2020-137).

div.head: Statistical analyses
div.p: The results are expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD), as indicated in the figure legends. Statistical significance was evaluated using two-tailed student's t-tests, with a P-value <0.05 deemed significant.

div.head: FOSL1 transcription is inhibited by KLF14
div.p: As high expressions of FOSL1 have been found to be crucial for glioma progression, this study explored the factors that regulate FOSL1. This study identified KLF14 as a transcription inhibitor of FOSL1 (Fig. 1A). Furthermore, overexpression of KLF14 decreased FOSL1 protein levels (Fig. 1B). This study also established KLF14-overexpressed stable cells and identified that either messenger RNA (mRNA) or protein levels of FOSL1 were decreased in KLF14-overexpressed cells (Fig. 1C and D). Conversely, FOSL1 mRNA and protein levels were upregulated in KLF14-knockdown stable cells (Fig. 1E and F). In addition, full-length KLF14, but not zinc finger 2 in KLF14 (ΔZF2) was found to bind to the FOSL1 promoter (Fig. 1G). These results demonstrate that KLF14 inhibits FOSL1 transcription.

div.head: KLF14 and FOSL1 are negatively correlated in glioma cancer
div.p: Previous studies discovered FOSL1 overexpression in glioma cancer, and so this study next performed immunohistochemistry staining of FOSL1 and KLF14 protein on tissue chips of human glioma cancers (Table 1). A significantly high protein level of FOSL1 but low protein level of KLF14 was observed in glioma cancers (Fig. 2A). Correlational analysis revealed a significant negative correlation between the protein expression levels of FOSL1 and KLF14 in glioma tumor tissues (Spearman's r = -0.4 and -0.6, respectively) (Fig. 2B). In addition, western blotting of FOSL1 and KLF14 in human glioma tissue demonstrated that FOSL1 was upregulated whereas KLF14 was downregulated in tumor than peri-tumor (Fig. 2C). These results indicate a negative correlation between FOSL1 and KLF14 in human glioma cancer.

div.head: KLF14 inhibits tumor proliferation and migration through FOSL1
div.p: The effect of KLF14 on GBM cell proliferation was verified by comparing cell growth between vector and KLF14-overexpression (OE) stable cells using the CCK-8 assay. Cell growth was lower in cells with KLF14-OE than in vector cells (Fig. 3A and B). The crystal violet staining assay demonstrated consistent results by indicating that cell proliferation was lower in KLF14-OE cells than in vector cells (Fig. 3C). Moreover, the transwell assay depicted that the migration rate was also lower in KLF14-OE cells than in vector cells (Fig. 3D). In addition, comparison of cell growth between KLF14 knockdown cells and control cells using the CCK-8 assay showed that cell growth was higher in cells with KLF14 knockdown than in control cells. However, knockdown of FOSL1 reversed the effect (Fig. 3E and F). The crystal violet staining assay confirmed these results and showed that cell proliferation was higher in KLF14 knockdown cells than in control cells, which was reversed with FOSL1 knockdown (Fig. 3G). Next, the results of the transwell assay suggested that KLF14 knockdown cells migrated quicker than control cells, and FOSL1 knockdown inhibited this trend (Fig. 3H). Collectively, these results indicate that KLF14 knockdown promotes GBM cell proliferation and migration caused by FOSL1 upregulation.

div.head: KLF14 inhibits tumor proliferation by inducing FOSL1-dependent EMT
div.p: When cancer cells undergo EMT, the Twist, Snail, Slug, and CD44 proteins are altered, thus causing cell migration and invasion. It has been reported that FOSL1 upregulates Snail2 and CD44 [24]. Therefore, this study assessed the expression of these factors to evaluate the phenotypic modulation of KLF14. KLF14-OE cells decreased the mRNA expression of Snail2 and CD44 (Fig. 4A and B). Knockdown of KLF14 in U87MG cells promoted the mRNA expression of Snail2 and CD44, which was reversed by FOSL1 knockdown (Fig. 4C). Consistent results were observed in U251MG cells (Fig. 4D). Furthermore, the protein levels of Snail2 and CD44 were upregulated in U87MG cells and U251MG cells with KLF14 knockdown, which was reversed by FOSL1 knockdown (Fig. 4E and F). These data suggest that KLF14 inhibits the metastasis of GBM cells by downregulating FOSL1.

div.head: Overexpression of KLF14 inhibits tumor proliferation in vivo
div.p: The role of KLF14 in GBM development in vivo was verified by establishing a xenograft tumor model for tumorigenesis experiments. U87MG cells stably overexpressing KLF14 and vector were subcutaneously injected into nude mice. KLF14-OE markedly decreased the tumorigenesis of GBM cells compared with the vector group (Fig. 5A). In addition, tumor weight was significantly lower in the KLF14overexpression group than in the control group (Fig. 5B). Similar results were observed in tumors from U251MG cells stably overexpressing KLF14 (Fig. 5C and D). Western blot assays of KLF14 and FOSL1 protein levels in tumor tissues proved that overexpression of KLF14 can inhibit the transcription of FOSL1 in glioma cells (Fig. 5E and F). These results confirm the role of KLF14 in inhibiting GBM in vivo.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: FOSL1 plays a carcinogenic role in GBM, and its inhibition is a prognostic and therapeutic option in GBM. However, there is a lack of research on the regulation of FOSL1. The present study confirmed that KLF14 inhibits FOSL1 transcription. KLF14 and FOSL1 are negatively correlated in glioma tissues. Overexpression of KLF14 reversed the effect of FOSL1 on cell invasion, migration and EMT in glioma cells. However, further studies are necessary to elucidate whether KLF14 targets FOSL1 directly.

Silencing FOSL1 inhibited tumor proliferation by decreasing the levels of EMT markers, such as Twist, Snail, Slug, and CD44. However, it remains unknown whether FOSL1 targets these factors directly or indirectly. FOSL1 is a component of the transcription factor AP-1 complex and thus may bind to the promoters of these markers to induce their expression. Exploring the mechanism by which FOSL1 regulates EMT is necessary to elucidate the role of FOSL1 as a target for treating CNS tumors.

A previous study showed that KLF14 depletion leads to spontaneous tumorigenesis in mice due to polo-like kinase 4 (PLK4)-dependent centrosome amplification in multiple human cancers [1]. However, nerve cells do not undergo cell division. Thus, it remains unknown whether KLF14 depletion leads to tumorigenesis in the CNS. This study demonstrated that the knockdown of KLF14 promotes cell invasion, migration, and EMT by upregulating FOSL1 in glioma cells, accompanied by the downregulation of Snail2 and CD44. Moreover, KLF14 overexpression inhibited tumor progression in vivo. These results suggest that KLF14 depletion may lead to spontaneous tumorigenesis in the nervous system. Furthermore, we will investigate the reasons for the decrease of KLF14 in gliomas to reveal the upstream molecular regulation mechanism of KLF14 in gliomas and uncover novel targets and strategies for glioma treatment. figure.head: Fig. 1 .
figure.figDesc: Fig. 1. FOSL1 transcription is inhibited by KLF14. (A) FOSL1-luc and KLF family (KLF1-17) plasmids were cotransfected into U87MG cells, and the relative FOSL1-luciferase activity was detected by a luciferase reporter assay. (B) Dosed KLF14 plasmids (2 μg and 4 μg) were transfected into U87MG cells, and the FOSL1 protein level was detected by western blotting. (C) qRT-PCR analysis of the mRNA expression level of FOSL1 in KLF14-OE U87MG cell lines constructed using lentivirus. (D) Western blot analysis of the expression level of FOSL1 in KLF14-OE U87MG cell lines constructed using lentivirus. (E) qRT-PCR analysis of the mRNA expression level of FOSL1 in KLF14 knockdown U87MG cell lines constructed using lentivirus. (F) Western blot analysis of the expression level of FOSL1 in KLF14 knockdown U87MG cell lines constructed using lentivirus. (G) U87MG cells transfected with vector (Control), Flag-KLF14 (WT), or Flag-KLF14-DZF2 (DZF2) were processed for ChIP using FLAG M2 beads. Coprecipitated chromatin DNA was analyzed by PCR using a primer pair that amplifies the -463 to -200 bp region of the FOSL1 promoter. Data represent mean ± SD, *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, Student's t-test.

figure.head: Fig. 2 .Fig. 3 .
figure.figDesc: Fig. 2. KLF14 and FOSL1 are negatively correlated in glioma cancer. (A) Comparison of FOSL1 and KLF14 protein expression by tissue array. Examples of immunohistochemical images of tumor tissue in glioma cancer stained with anti-FOSL1 and anti-KLF14 antibodies, respectively (scale bar, 100 μm). (B) Spearman's r-coefficient test for evaluation of correlations between FOSL1 and KLF14 immunohistochemical expression status in glioma cancer tissues. ρ indicates a negative correlation. The level of signification is expressed by the P-value. (C) Western blot analysis of the expression levels of FOSL1 and KLF14 in glioma cancer tissues.

figure.head: Fig. 4 .
figure.figDesc: Fig. 4. KLF14 inhibits tumor proliferation by inducing FOSL1-dependent EMT. (A and B) mRNA expression of Snail2 and CD44 in KLF14-OE U87MG (A) and U251MG (B) cells determined by RT-qPCR. (C and D) mRNA expression of Snail2 and CD44 in KLF14 knockdown or KLF14 and FOSL1 double knockdown U87MG (C) and U251MG (D) cells determined by RT-qPCR. (E and F) Protein expression of Twist, Snail, Slug, and CD44 in KLF14 knockdown or KLF14 and FOSL1 double knockdown U87MG (A) and U251MG (B) cells determined by western blotting.

figure.head: Fig. 5 .
figure.figDesc: Fig. 5. Overexpression of KLF14 inhibits tumor proliferation in vivo. (A) After injecting KLF14-OEU87MG cells in nude mice, the tumors were collected four weeks later. (B) The tumor volume was measured after four weeks. (C) After injecting KLF14-OEU251MG cells in nude mice, the tumors were collected four weeks later. (D) The tumor volume was measured after four weeks. (E and F) KLF14 and FOSL1 protein levels were detected in tumor tissues by western blotting. Data represent mean ± SD, *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, Student's t-test.
